title: Sounds, Spelling, and the Capital Letter
summary: The four letters German writes beyond the Latin twenty-six, the three diphthongs, what the spelling says about vowel length, the consonants that do not sound as an English reader expects, and the capital letter that marks every noun.

script.heading: The letters German adds to the Latin alphabet

letters.name: o-Umlaut
letters.approx: front tongue, rounded lips; the vowel of French *peu*

letters.name: u-Umlaut
letters.approx: front tongue, rounded lips; the vowel of French *mur*

letters.name: Eszett, scharfes s
letters.notes: Follows a long vowel or a diphthong, and so never opens a word.

notes: The remaining twenty-six letters are those of the Latin alphabet.
The umlauted letters have capitals — Ä, Ö, Ü. The ß was originally a small letter only; its use as a capital is now permitted.
Three pairs of letters stand for a single vowel sound apiece: **ei** and **ai** for [aɪ], **au** for [aʊ], **eu** and **äu** for [ɔʏ].

rules.heading: The alphabet
rules.statement: German writes the twenty-six letters of the Latin alphabet and four more: **ä**, **ö**, **ü** and **ß**. The first three are a, o and u carrying the Umlaut; the fourth is called *Eszett* or *scharfes s*.

rules.heading: The vowel ä
rules.statement: Short **ä** is [ɛ], the vowel of English *head*, and is identical with short e. Long **ä** is [ɛː] in the prescribed standard, though over much of the north it is said the same as long e.
footnotes: The [ɛː] pronunciation is most often kept where it distinguishes a subjunctive from an indicative — *gäbe* against *gebe*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §23.1.5, p. 505, for the two values of ä and the northern merger with long e.

rules.heading: ä before r
rules.statement: Where **r** follows, **ä** is heard as the vowel of English *air*.

rules.heading: The vowel ö
rules.statement: **ö** is a front vowel said with rounded lips: the tongue stands as for *e*, the lips as for *o*. It is [øː] when long and [œ] when short — the vowel of French *peu*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: The phonetic alphabet, p. xvi: *Hölle* [œ], *Höhle* / French *peu* [øː].

sources.citation: *Close-mid front rounded vowel*, Wikipedia.
sources.note: Cited for the articulation: front tongue position, close-mid height, rounded lips.

rules.heading: The vowel ü
rules.statement: **ü** is a front vowel said with rounded lips: the tongue stands as for *i*, the lips as for *u*. It is [yː] when long and [ʏ] when short — the vowel of French *mur*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: The phonetic alphabet, p. xvi: *Fülle* [ʏ], *Mühle* / French *mur* [yː].

sources.citation: *Close front rounded vowel*, Wikipedia.
sources.note: Cited for the articulation: front tongue position, close height, rounded lips.

rules.heading: The letter ß
rules.statement: **ß** stands for a voiceless *s*. It follows a long vowel or a diphthong, and so never opens a word; after a short vowel the same sound is written **ss**.
footnotes: Switzerland makes no such distinction and writes ss throughout.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §23.4, pp. 511–512, for the distribution of ss and ß and for Swiss usage.

rules.heading: The capital that opens a sentence
rules.statement: The first word of a German sentence carries a capital letter, whatever part of speech it belongs to.

rules.heading: The capital that marks a noun
rules.statement: Every noun carries a capital letter, wherever it stands in the sentence and without exception. A word standing in lower case inside a sentence is therefore not a noun.

examples.gloss: The man is reading a book.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §23.2.1, pp. 506–510, on capitals with nouns and proper names.

rules.heading: ch as the ich-Laut
rules.statement: After the front vowels i, e, ü and ö, after **l** and **r**, and in the suffix **-chen**, **ch** is the *ich-Laut* [ç], close to the *sh* of English *ship*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: ch as the ach-Laut
rules.statement: After the back vowels a, o and u, **ch** is the *ach-Laut* [x], the other of the two values the pair carries (¶9).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The diphthong eu, äu
rules.statement: **eu** stands for [ɔʏ], the vowel of English *boy*, and not for the *ew* an English reader would supply. **äu** spells the same diphthong.
footnotes: The two spellings are distributed by derivation rather than by sound: **äu** appears where the word is related to one with **au** — *Haus*, *Häuser*; *Maus*, *Mäuse*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
*German orthography*, Wikipedia.

rules.heading: The diphthong ei, ai
rules.statement: **ei** stands for [aɪ], the vowel of English *eye*. **ai** spells the same diphthong.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: The phonetic alphabet, p. xvi: *fein* [aɪ], English *fine*.

sources.citation: *German orthography*, Wikipedia.

rules.heading: The spelling ie
rules.statement: **ie** is not a diphthong: it stands for a single long [iː], the vowel of English *see*. It is the usual spelling for that vowel.
footnotes: The order of the two letters decides the sound, and the two orders are two different words: *Miene* [iː] against *meine* [aɪ] (¶12).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §23.1.4(e)(iii), p. 505: long [iː] is most commonly spelled ie.

rules.heading: The diphthong au
rules.statement: **au** stands for [aʊ], the vowel of English *mouse*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: The phonetic alphabet, p. xvi: *Maus* [aʊ], English *mouse*.

rules.heading: Vowel length and the consonants after it
rules.statement: A vowel is short before a doubled consonant and usually short before a cluster of consonants; before a single consonant it is usually long. **ß** counts as a single consonant, which is what *Fuß* against *Fluss* rests on (¶6).

examples.note: long; ß counts as one consonant

paradigms.caption: What follows the vowel, and how long the vowel is
paradigms.footnote: k is never doubled; **ck** is written instead — *Acker*, *Pack*.

footnotes: The cluster rule has common exceptions which keep a long vowel: *Art*, *Mond*, *Jagd*, *atmen*. An inflected or derived form also keeps the length of the word it comes from — *Tag*, *Tags*; *lösen*, *löste*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: Length written into the spelling
rules.statement: A long vowel can be marked by a silent **h** after it, especially before m, n, l and r, or by doubling the vowel letter. A vowel standing alone at the end of a word is long.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: b, d and g at the end
rules.statement: At the end of a word or syllable, and before a consonant, **b**, **d** and **g** are said as [p], [t] and [k]. Elsewhere — at the start of a word, or between vowels — they keep their English values.
footnotes: Across the northern two-thirds of Germany a final **g** is widely said as the *ach-Laut* or the *ich-Laut* instead — *Zug*, *sagt* (¶9, ¶10). This is not the prescribed standard.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The ending -ig
rules.statement: In the ending **-ig** the g is said as the *ich-Laut* [ç] (¶9), not as [k].

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The letter s
rules.statement: At the start of a word before a vowel, and between vowels, **s** is voiced [z]. Everywhere else it is [s].

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: sp and st at the start of a word
rules.statement: At the start of a word, **sp** and **st** are said [ʃp] and [ʃt] — the s becomes the *sh* sound.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The pair ng
rules.statement: **ng** is always [ŋ] alone, never [ŋg]. German *Finger* has the ng of English *singer*, not the ng of English *finger*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

rules.heading: The letters v, w and z
rules.statement: Three letters carry values an English reader will not expect: **w** is [v], **v** is [f], and **z** is [ts].

paradigms.caption: The three letters and their values

footnotes: In loan-words that are not final, **v** keeps [v] — *Vase*, *Klavier*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: The phonetic alphabet, p. xvi: *wann* [v], English *van*.

sources.citation: *German orthography*, Wikipedia.

rules.heading: Word stress
rules.statement: In most native German words the stress falls on the first syllable, and it stays on that syllable whatever endings are added to the word.
footnotes: The prefixes be-, emp-, ent-, er-, ge-, ver- and zer- are never stressed, so a word carrying one is stressed on the syllable after it — *verstehen*, *Geschichte*. The suffix **-ei** is always stressed: *Bäckerei*.
The commonest native words that break the first-syllable rule are *Forelle*, *Holunder*, *Hornisse*, *Kartoffel*, *lebendig* and *Wacholder*.

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.

drills.stem: In which word is **ch** the *ach-Laut*?
drills.explanation: *Buch* has u before the ch, and a back vowel gives the *ach-Laut* [x] (¶10). The other three have i or r in front of it, which gives the *ich-Laut* [ç] (¶9).

drills.stem: In which of these is **ch** the *ich-Laut*?
drills.explanation: *welche* has e before the ch and *Milch* has l, and both environments give [ç] (¶9). *doch* and *Achtung* have the back vowels o and a, which give [x] (¶10).

drills.stem: Pair each word with the value **ch** carries in it and the reason.
drills.explanation: *Buch* and *Achtung* have back vowels before the ch, so both take [x] (¶10). *Milch* has l and *echt* has the front vowel e, so both take [ç] — but for different reasons, and the pairing has to say which (¶9). No environment gives [x] after l or r, which is what rules out the fourth label.

drills.stem: In which word does **ä** have the vowel of English *air*?
drills.explanation: An r after the ä gives it the *air* vowel (¶3). None of the other three has an r following, so the ä keeps its ordinary value (¶2).

drills.stem: Which English vowel is closest to the **ä** of *Äpfel*?
drills.explanation: Short ä is [ɛ], which is the vowel of *head*, and is the same sound as short e (¶2).

drills.stem: How is the **ü** of *Müller* made?
options: the tongue as for *u*, the lips spread as for *i*
the tongue as for *i*, the lips rounded as for *u*
the tongue as for *e*, the lips rounded as for *o*
the tongue and the lips both as for *u*
drills.explanation: ü is a front vowel with rounded lips: the tongue is where it stands for *i*, the lips are where they stand for *u* (¶5). The third option describes ö instead (¶4), which is the confusion the two letters invite.

drills.stem: Which French word carries the vowel of German *schön*?
drills.explanation: Long ö is [øː], the vowel of French *peu* (¶4). *mur* has [yː], which is German ü (¶5).

drills.stem: In which words is the marked vowel made with the tongue forward and the lips rounded?
drills.explanation: ö and ü are both front vowels with rounded lips (¶4, ¶5). *Straße* has a, which is neither front nor rounded.

drills.stem: Three of these could be German words as they are spelled. Which could not?
drills.explanation: ß follows a long vowel or a diphthong, so nothing can precede it at the start of a word and no German word opens with it (¶6).

drills.stem: German writes the twenty-six letters of the Latin alphabet and adds some of its own. How many letters does the German alphabet add?
drills.explanation: ä, ö, ü and ß (¶1).

drills.stem: Which of these letters does German write in addition to the Latin twenty-six?
drills.explanation: German adds ä, ö, ü and ß (¶1). The ø belongs to Danish and Norwegian; German rounds the same vowel with the Umlaut instead, as ö (¶4).

drills.stem: Which words in **Ich mag die Katzen** are nouns?
drills.explanation: *Katzen* carries a capital inside the sentence, which only a noun does (¶8). *Ich* carries one because it opens the sentence, and that says nothing about its part of speech (¶7).

drills.stem: A word stands in the middle of a German sentence in lower case. What does that establish?
options: it is a noun of a kind that keeps its small letter
drills.explanation: Nouns take a capital without exception, so a small letter inside a sentence rules the word out as a noun (¶8).

drills.stem: In **Dein Buch ist interessant**, why does *Dein* carry a capital?
options: because it stands first in the sentence
because it belongs to a noun
because it is addressed to a person
drills.explanation: The first word of a sentence is capitalised whatever its part of speech (¶7). *Buch* in the same sentence carries its capital for the other reason — it is a noun (¶8).

drills.stem: Pair each word with the sound of its marked vowel.
columnII: front tongue, rounded lips — as in French *peu*
front tongue, rounded lips — as in French *mur*
drills.explanation: ö goes with *peu* and ü with *mur*, and swapping them is the first wrong pairing (¶4, ¶5). *Äpfel* has plain short ä (¶2) while *März* has the r that turns it into the *air* vowel (¶3).

drills.stem: Which English word carries the vowel of German *Leute*?
drills.explanation: **eu** is [ɔʏ], the vowel of *boy* — not the *ew* the spelling suggests to an English reader (¶11).

drills.stem: In which words does the spelling stand for [ɔʏ]?
drills.explanation: **eu** and **äu** both spell [ɔʏ] (¶11). *Bauer* has **au**, which is [aʊ] (¶14) — the Umlaut over the a is exactly what separates the two.

drills.stem: German **mein** rhymes with which English word?
drills.explanation: **ei** is [aɪ], the vowel of *eye* (¶12).

drills.stem: Pair each word with the vowel its spelling stands for.
drills.explanation: **ie** is a single long [iː] (¶13); **ei** and **ai** are both the diphthong [aɪ] (¶12). So *Lied* and *Miene* go together, and *Seite* and *Mai* go together — the order of the two letters is the whole difference.

drills.stem: *Miene* and *meine* are two different words. How do they differ in sound?
options: both have [iː]; only the spelling differs
both have [aɪ]; only the spelling differs
drills.explanation: **ie** is long [iː] (¶13) and **ei** is the diphthong [aɪ] (¶12), so reversing the two letters changes the vowel outright.

drills.stem: Which word carries the vowel of English *mouse*?
drills.explanation: **au** is [aʊ] (¶14). *Leute* and *Läufer* have [ɔʏ] (¶11) and *Lied* has [iː] (¶13).

drills.stem: In which of these words is the vowel short?
drills.explanation: A doubled consonant makes the vowel before it short, and *bitte* has tt (¶15). The other three have a single consonant after the vowel, which usually leaves it long.

drills.stem: *Fuß* and *Fluss* end in the same sound, spelled differently. What does the difference in spelling record?
options: the vowel of *Fuß* is long and the vowel of *Fluss* is short
the vowel of *Fuß* is short and the vowel of *Fluss* is long
nothing about the sound; the two spellings are regional variants
drills.explanation: ß follows a long vowel and ss a short one (¶6), and this is the same rule as the one that makes a vowel short before a doubled consonant (¶15): ß counts as a single consonant, ss as a double one.

drills.stem: In which words does the spelling mark the vowel as long?
drills.explanation: A silent h marks length in *fahren*, a doubled vowel letter in *Schnee*, and a vowel alone at the end of a word is long in *wo* (¶16). *Klasse* has a doubled consonant, which makes the vowel short (¶15).

drills.stem: How does the **d** of *Rad* sound?
drills.explanation: b, d and g are said as [p], [t] and [k] at the end of a word (¶17). In *Rades*, where the d falls between vowels, it is [d] again.

drills.stem: In which words does the marked consonant lose its voice?
drills.explanation: *Sieb* and *Zug* end in b and g, and the g of *sagt* stands before a consonant; all three are said [p], [k], [k] (¶17). In *geben* the b falls between vowels and stays [b].

drills.stem: How does *König* end?
options: with [k], as b, d and g do at the end of a word
drills.explanation: The ending **-ig** takes the *ich-Laut* (¶18), which is the exception to the rule that a final g is [k] (¶17). It is the *ich-Laut* rather than the *ach-Laut* because the vowel before it is i (¶9).

drills.stem: In which word is **s** voiced, as the z of English *zero*?
drills.explanation: s between vowels is [z] (¶19). In *lassen* it is doubled, in *Haus* it is final, and in *Wespe* it stands before a consonant — all [s].

drills.stem: How does *Straße* begin?
drills.explanation: At the start of a word, st is [ʃt] (¶20). The same word ends in ß, which marks the vowel before it as long (¶6, ¶15).

drills.stem: German *Finger* and English *finger* are spelled alike. How does the German **ng** differ?
options: it is [ŋ] alone, as in English *singer*
it is [ŋg], with the g sounded separately
it is [n] followed by [g], as two sounds
the g is silent and the n is lengthened
drills.explanation: ng is always [ŋ] in German and never [ŋg] (¶21), so *Finger* has the ng of *singer* rather than of *finger*.

drills.stem: Pair each word with the sound its marked consonant carries.
drills.explanation: w is [v] and v is [f], and swapping them is the first wrong pairing (¶22). *Sonne* opens with s before a vowel, which is [z] (¶19).

drills.stem: Native German words are stressed on one syllable, and adding endings does not move it. Counting from the left, which syllable of **Glaubhaftigkeit** carries the stress?
drills.explanation: The stress is on *Glaub-*, the first syllable, exactly where it falls in *glauben* — the endings piled on after it change nothing (¶23).

drills.stem: *Arbeit* is stressed on its first syllable. Where is *verstehen* stressed?
drills.explanation: The first-syllable rule holds for native words, but ver- is one of the prefixes that is never stressed, so the stress falls on the syllable after it (¶23).

sources.citation: Durrell, Martin, *Hammer's German Grammar and Usage*, 5th edn. London: Routledge, 2011.
sources.note: §§23.1.1–23.1.6 (pp. 502–507) on spelling and pronunciation, §23.2.1 (pp. 506–510) on capitals, §23.4 (pp. 511–512) on ss and ß.
